doc.title: Bobby Shew interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 1, 2020

chapter: Studio craft and the TV and rock dates
title: Rock dates with no written music; overdubbing a brass section
summary: Shew describes building horn parts by ear over rhythm tracks, and overdubbing trumpets and trombones for several paychecks.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: Were those rock & roll dates different? Did you ever show up to do a date and there was no music? Like you were expected to come up with horn parts?

Boy did I ever. Yeah. A lot of them were like that. And there was this one guy, what the hell was his name, I’ve suppressed his name purposely I guess. But I would show up, myself and the saxophone player would show up and they’d have all these rhythm tracks and you’d start listening to them. And then, “What do you guys feel? What do you feel? What do you feel?” You know? You’d have to sit there and, “How about this?” [scats] Oh yeah I like that, I like that. So we’re looking at each other and going let’s get this thing done and get the hell out of here.
Yeah, I’ve had that experience. I wonder if when you had to do that, was there a vocal you were hearing?
Because you don’t want to be —
You don’t want to get in the way.
Yeah you don’t want to be getting in the way, right.

Well the other thing is I did one time for this one guy and — I can’t remember his name but he was a noteworthy producer out there, a rock & roll guy. And those people I did not enjoy working with very much. But this guy, he heard that I played trombone also. So I had to bring my trombone in there and my trumpet, and a flugelhorn. And when I got in there there was nothing but a track. And so we’d figure out, and I’d have to figure it all out by my ear. And I’d sing it to him and I’d put my horn or I’d put a mute in and I’d play along with the track in the booth and he’d say yeah that’s good right there, I like that, that’s good. No let’s leave that open right there. And I’d go through it a few times and I’m trying to remember what the hell did I do you know. And you have to go in there, but the good thing about that is that they stop the tape and they can go back and keep punching in and punch out. So one track would take a whole afternoon, like four hours or five hours. Because I would finally put the first trumpet part on the way we wanted it. Then I’d go back in and put a second trumpet part on, and maybe a third trumpet part on, and then I’d pick up the trombone and I’d put on three trombone parts. And I would build an entire brass section myself. The good news about that is for every person that I record for I have to get paid as an individual so I got paid six salaries for an afternoon. And one salary for a session would be say like $450 or $500 so you’re making like three grand for an afternoon. You know.
Well that helps. Even though you might have had wrinkles on your forehead —
